resources.string: DNS protection · No ads · No tracking
DNS protection through a local VPN

DNSBunker blocks ads, trackers and scam or malware sites for all apps on your device. For this, Android sets up a local VPN connection: it only receives the address lookups (DNS) and sends them encrypted to dnsbunker.org. The rest of your internet traffic keeps going directly to its destination, no outside server sees it. Apps with their own DNS can bypass this protection. Another VPN will be replaced. The app sends no telemetry.
Standard mode protects system DNS. Enable public port-53 interception under Wi-Fi for broader coverage. Apps using their own encrypted DNS can bypass either mode.
Protection stays on for unknown Wi-Fi networks. Only networks you explicitly add are exempt.
On exempt Wi-Fi, the network handles DNS. The app cannot verify its encryption. Wi-Fi names can be impersonated.
Connections to devices on your local network remain direct. The app routes only DNS traffic to its virtual DNS addresses.
Local names such as nas.home.arpa never go to DNSBunker. This switch lets them be resolved only with the additional permissions below.
Resolve local names through the private DNS server only on explicitly trusted Wi-Fi.
Trust this Wi-Fi for local names
Without consent, local lookups fail safely. Optional router DNS uses unencrypted UDP on the local network. Public DNSBunker connections remain encrypted.
The DNSBunker tunnel will stop on this Wi-Fi. The network will handle DNS; the app cannot verify its encryption. Wi-Fi names can be impersonated.
Names such as nas.home.arpa are sent to the private DNS server only on trusted Wi-Fi. These local queries are unencrypted and visible on the network. Public queries to DNSBunker remain encrypted.

Counted as blocked is an answer that DNSBunker marks as blocked (HaGeZi Pro, HaGeZi TIF or DNSBunker’s own list). A domain that simply does not exist is not counted. The app’s own check queries are excluded.
EDNS padding rounds query sizes to 128-byte blocks. It does not hide domain names.
Check DNS resolution periodically and attempt recovery after connection failures.
If DoH fails, try DNSBunker over certificate-verified TLS on port 853. No public plaintext fallback.
This app connects to DNSBunker using DoH/2, HTTP/3, DoT or DoQ with certificate verification. If encrypted resolution fails, it does not silently switch to public plaintext DNS.
No ads, no trackers, no account. Settings stay on your device. DNS queries are sent encrypted to dnsbunker.org for resolution.

HTTP/3 and DoQ use QUIC. If UDP is blocked, HTTPS over TCP/443 remains an option. Direct IP connections without hostname SNI help with some SNI blocks. They cannot bypass blocked server IPs or a pending Wi-Fi login.
Open Android Wi-Fi sign-in. If the sign-in page doesn’t load, turn on “Allow Wi-Fi sign-in pages” in the settings or pause protection briefly.

DNSBunker receives the DNS question and sees your public source IP to resolve it. The connection is encrypted. The linked official policy covers service-side processing. This app stores no domain names and sends no telemetry. Settings stay local; counters and the 2-hour chart stay only in memory until process exit or reset. Wi-Fi names are stored only for rules you explicitly set. Android backups are disabled. Optional router DNS is separately permitted, unencrypted local UDP. If you turn it on, recently blocked domains are kept in memory only. Excluded apps are stored on the device only. If encrypted DNS fails, the app may look up dnsbunker.org through the network’s DNS and load a status notice from dnsbunker.org.
Counters and the chart in this app will reset. No domain names are stored.
Since app start · only on this device
Ads, trackers and dangerous sites are blocked in all apps, and your lookups are encrypted.

Redirects public UDP/TCP port-53 queries to DNSBunker. The local IP tunnel also handles ordinary TCP/UDP traffic for this. Local networks remain directly reachable. Other apps’ own DoH/DoT can still bypass DNS filtering.
The IP stack is unavailable on this device. Comprehensive interception cannot be enabled.

In comprehensive mode, other packets also stay on-device: the app connects directly to the original destination and keeps no connection logs. Other apps’ TLS remains unchanged; there is no remote VPN exit.
A battery-optimization exemption can reduce background disconnections. Android or the device vendor may still stop the app. Continuous operation can use more battery.
Private DNS can bypass this local DNS protection and cause warnings or incomplete statistics. It should be off during normal app use. The app does not change this system setting itself.

The block lists come from HaGeZi: the Pro list covers ad networks, analytics and telemetry, the Threat Intelligence Feed (TIF) covers phishing, scam and malware domains. The assignment comes from the marker DNSBunker sends with each blocked answer. A blocked query does not prove that an attack was prevented.
Warm DNS timings exclude initial connection setup. Total wait includes handshake, queueing, retries and fallback. These are network timings, not pure server processing time.

Use DNSBunker without the app VPN
Wi-Fi exceptions need the location permission and location turned on. Otherwise Android hides the network name.
Exceptions are paused while Android’s “Block connections without VPN” is on.
Protection restarts automatically after updates and restarts. For even more reliability, select DNSBunker as always-on VPN in Android.
Another VPN or Android ended DNSBunker. Tap to turn protection back on.
Exceptions apply right after a restart only if Android allows location access “all the time”. Otherwise they start working once you open the app.
Checks GitHub once a day for a new version. GitHub sees your IP address for this.
The update failed. Try again later or download it from the website.
Allow DNSBunker to install apps, then tap “Update now” again.
DNSBunker %1$s is available. Tap to update.
DNSBunker’s certificates are valid for only a few days. If your device clock is off, encrypted DNS cannot be verified and no names can be resolved. Set date and time to automatic.
Tap to finish installing the DNSBunker update.
Until %1$s. Protection turns back on automatically.
During the pause your device uses the network’s normal DNS, unencrypted and without DNSBunker’s filter. Useful for Wi-Fi login pages or when a site doesn’t load.
Android reports no working internet connection for this network. Check Wi-Fi or mobile data.
Your internet works, but the DNSBunker server does not respond. This can be a server outage or a block in this network. The app keeps trying automatically.
The server is reachable but currently does not answer encrypted DNS queries. The app keeps trying automatically.
Android already sends your DNS queries encrypted to DNSBunker, even without the app’s protection. Statistics, Wi-Fi and app exceptions are only available with the app’s protection.
Android already sends DNS queries to DNSBunker itself. Together with the app’s protection this can distort statistics and Wi-Fi exceptions. Use only one of the two.
Since Android 9, Android itself can talk to DNSBunker encrypted (“Private DNS”). It takes no VPN slot and also works next to another VPN.
Open the settings › Network & internet (on Samsung: Connections › More connection settings) › Private DNS › “Private DNS provider hostname” › enter the hostname below.
Without the app VPN there are no statistics, no Wi-Fi or app exceptions and no pause. Turn off the app’s protection when you use Private DNS.
Keeps the last blocked domains in memory only, to help you find false positives. The list is cleared on reset and when the app closes, and never leaves your device.
Nothing blocked since the list was turned on.
Is %1$s blocked by mistake? Listseek shows which HaGeZi list contains the domain and helps you report it.
Excluded apps bypass the protection and use the network’s normal DNS, unencrypted and unfiltered. Useful for apps that have problems with DNSBunker, for example banking or work apps.
With “Block connections without VPN”, excluded apps have no internet unless Android allows them separately.
This Wi-Fi needs a sign-in. DNSBunker steps aside until then and turns protection back on automatically afterwards.

Detects sign-in pages in hotels, trains or cafés and lets them load without DNSBunker. Only when encrypted DNS does not work on that network. Protection returns automatically once the Wi-Fi is unlocked.
Ad and tracking addresses from the HaGeZi Pro list are never reached, in apps, games and the browser. That also saves data and battery.
Phishing, scam and malware sites from the HaGeZi Threat Intelligence Feed are blocked before a connection is made.
Your mobile operator or the Wi-Fi no longer sees which addresses you look up. DNSBunker keeps no query logs.

How it works: before an app loads anything, it asks for the address (DNS), like looking up a phone book. DNSBunker answers these questions and lets unwanted addresses run into nothing. All other traffic goes straight to the internet.
Local domain of this network: %1$s. Names under it never go to DNSBunker.
